newsitem.title: INDIA: Woes keep mounting for Indian prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Woes keep mounting for Indian prime minister.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's retreat on Wednesday over an insurance bill is the latest in a series of setbacks that reflect a tenuous grip on power and an uncertain future for his coalition.
"I think he's just biding his time now," independent political analyst Rasheed Talib said after Gujral abruptly withdrew an insurance regulatory bill from parliament.
"He is settling into the role of being a kind of benign chairman, emeritus of the board, a figurehead. It's a shocking state of affairs," Talib said.

Gujral retracted the bill, which would create an insurance watchdog, after failing to attract enough support to defeat an opposition-backed amendment to bar foreign firms from the state-controlled insurance sector.

Earlier in the day, Gujral's communist allies voted against the government on another amendment, lining up against the rest of the centre-left United Front coalition for the first time since it assumed power 14 months ago.

The opposition to the bill from both the rightwing opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Gujral's leftwing partners underscored lingering divisions over the opening up of India's market to private companies.
The insurance industry is controlled by state firms, and the government in its 1997/98 (April-March) budget proposed allowing a few Indian firms into the health insurance sector.

Foreign countries led by the United States have been pressing India hard to open up its lucrative insurance sector, arguing the move would boost domestic savings and generate much needed funds for expensive infrastructure projects.
"I don't want this house to be a surrogate of a foreign power," Samata Party leader George Fernandes, a BJP ally, said, summing up the view of many deputies on the Left and Right.
The politburo of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) said "patriotic forces...have been opposing the move to privatise the insurance sector as this would be detrimental to India's self-reliance".

A senior official in the Finance Ministry, which has been spearheading the government's drive to press ahead with free-market economic reforms, said: "Is this the signal we are sending to foreign investors?"
"We are extremely disappointed," George Otto, chief representative at the India liaison office of Germany's Allianz AG Holding, said.

Gujral's plight was compounded by the absence from parliament of many legislators from the Congress party, which provides make-or-break support to the prime minister but holds no government portfolios.
Many Congress deputies were headed to Calcutta where the party is holding a crucial meeting starting on Friday.
Members of Gujral's United Front coalition privately criticised the government for failing to prepare the political ground for the vote.

Vinod Mehta, editor of Outlook magazine, said it was the latest embarrassment for Gujral, who was heckled at a meeting last weekend of his own party. "Gujral's diminishing clout is not unconcealed," Mehta said.
As with insurance, the communists and the BJP have opposed a proposal, backed by Gujral and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, to raise oil prices to plug a mounting subsidy bill.
The proposal has been hanging fire for months while the government struggles to allay the leftwing parties' worries.
Gujral, who assumed office in April, has also had to retreat over a bill to reserve seats in parliament for women and proposals to raise government employees' salaries.
